introduction-the-limitation-of-load-aver.core: Load average mixes CPU demand and I/O waits in one number, is unnormalised and smoothed over minutes, and says nothing about how much work is actually delayed. Pressure Stall Information (PSI, Linux 4.20+) directly measures the percentage of time tasks were stalled waiting for CPU, memory or I/O, over 10-, 60- and 300-second windows plus a cumulative total, system-wide and per cgroup. It answers 'how much is contention hurting us?'.

first_principles.problem: Load average rises to 20, but nobody knows whether it's CPU, memory or disk causing slowness.

analogy.title: Measuring time spent waiting in each queue
analogy.story: Instead of counting people in the building, measure how long they wait at the lift, the canteen and the printer.
analogy.breaks: Queues are visible; PSI is inferred from task stalls.

code.text:
cat /proc/pressure/cpu
# some avg10=45.20 avg60=38.11 avg300=20.05 total=987654321
cat /proc/pressure/io
# some avg10=2.10 ... full avg10=0.50 ...
# → CPU contention, not disk

check.q: What does PSI measure that load average doesn't?
check.a: The percentage of time tasks were actually stalled waiting on a specific resource (CPU, memory or I/O).

the-interface-procpressure.core: Each /proc/pressure file reports 'some' and 'full' lines with avg10, avg60 and avg300 percentages and total, the cumulative stall microseconds, which is ideal for rate() in Prometheus. Processes can also register triggers: open the file, write 'some 150000 1000000' (150 ms of stall in a 1 s window), and poll() for events. That's how systemd-oomd, Android's lmkd and autoscalers react to pressure in near real time.

first_principles.problem: A team wants to react within seconds when memory pressure spikes, not wait for minute-level metrics.

analogy.title: A meter with a buzzer setting
analogy.story: You can read the meter whenever, or set it to buzz when waiting exceeds a threshold in any second.
analogy.breaks: Buzzers are simple; triggers need a process polling the file.

code.text:
rate(node_pressure_memory_waiting_seconds_total[1m])     # fraction of time some task waited
rate(node_pressure_memory_stalled_seconds_total[1m])     # 'full' stall fraction
# alert if > 0.10 for 5m

check.q: Why use PSI's 'total' field rather than avg values for monitoring systems?
check.a: It's a cumulative counter of stall time, so you can compute exact rates over any window with rate().

some-vs-full-pressure.core: 'some' is the share of time at least one task was stalled on the resource, so some work was delayed. 'full' is the share of time all non-idle tasks were stalled at once, so the system made no productive progress. full is the stronger signal of severe trouble such as thrashing or I/O storms. CPU full is reported as zero at system level (CPU can't be fully stalled while something runs) but is meaningful per cgroup.

first_principles.problem: An engineer sees memory 'some' at 30% and panics, though 'full' is near zero and throughput is fine.
truths: Partial delay differs from total stall.

analogy.title: Some cars waiting vs total gridlock
analogy.story: Some cars waiting at lights is normal friction; every car stopped is gridlock.
analogy.breaks: Traffic is visible; stalls are measured per task.

example.title: Interpretation
flow: memory some avg10=30, full avg10=0.5 → reclaim friction, OK
memory full avg10=25 → thrashing, act now
cpu some 50 → CPU contention, add cores

check.q: What does a high 'full' memory pressure value indicate?
check.a: All non-idle tasks were simultaneously stalled waiting on memory, so the system was making no useful progress (e.g. thrashing).

interpreting-cpu-pressure.core: CPU pressure 'some' is the percentage of time runnable tasks waited for a CPU, which is run-queue contention. Low values (<5–10%) are normal; sustained high values mean more demand than cores, or CPU quota throttling in a cgroup (cpu.max), which appears as cgroup CPU pressure even when the host has idle CPUs. Remedies: add capacity, reduce demand, raise quotas, or spread work.

first_principles.problem: A container is slow with node CPU at 40%, and its cgroup CPU pressure is 60% because of a tight CPU limit.
truths: Quotas throttle even with idle CPUs.

analogy.title: Waiting for a free checkout
analogy.story: You may wait because all tills are busy, or because your store policy limits you to one till even when others are free.
analogy.breaks: Store policies are visible; quotas are hidden in cgroup files.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Raise limit to 2 CPUs; pressure drops.

code.text:
cg=/sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/<pod>.slice
cat $cg/cpu.pressure          # some avg10=61.0
grep -E 'nr_throttled|throttled_usec' $cg/cpu.stat
cat $cg/cpu.max               # 100000 100000 → 1 CPU limit

check.q: How can a container show high CPU pressure while the node has idle CPUs?
check.a: Its cgroup CPU quota (limit) throttles it, so its tasks wait despite free host CPUs.

interpreting-memory-pressure.core: Memory pressure measures time spent stalled on memory: direct reclaim (the allocating task frees memory itself), refaulting recently evicted pages (workingset thrashing), swap-ins and compaction. 'some' rising means allocations are getting slower; 'full' rising means thrashing. It's the best early warning before OOM, used by systemd-oomd and earlyoom, and per-cgroup values show which workload is squeezed.

first_principles.problem: A node slowly becomes unresponsive with no OOM kill, because it's thrashing on page cache refaults.

analogy.title: A kitchen constantly clearing counter space
analogy.story: Cooks spend more time moving things back and forth to the pantry than actually cooking.
analogy.breaks: Cooks notice; kernels need PSI to quantify.

code.text:
cat /proc/pressure/memory
# full avg10=32.5 → thrashing
grep -E 'workingset_refault_file|pgmajfault' /proc/vmstat
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/batch.slice/memory.pressure

check.q: Why is memory PSI a better early warning than free memory?
check.a: It measures actual time lost to reclaim and refaults, revealing thrashing that free-memory numbers don't show.

interpreting-io-pressure.core: I/O pressure measures time tasks were stalled waiting on block I/O: reads, synchronous writes, fsync, and page faults that hit disk. High 'some' means I/O latency affects work; high 'full' means everything is waiting on storage. Combine it with iostat (await, %util, queue depth) and per-cgroup io.pressure to find the noisy workload, then fix with faster storage, caching, I/O limits (io.max or io.weight) or fewer synchronous writes.

first_principles.problem: A nightly backup makes the database slow, and node-level metrics don't show which workload is suffering.

analogy.title: A single loading dock shared by two warehouses
analogy.story: When one is unloading a huge shipment, the other's trucks wait in line.
analogy.breaks: Docks are visible; I/O stalls need PSI and iostat.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: DB I/O pressure drops during backups.

code.text:
cat /proc/pressure/io                         # some avg10=48
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/postgresql.service/io.pressure   # victim
iostat -x 1 3 | grep nvme0n1                  # await 45 ms, util 99%
systemctl set-property backup.service IOWeight=10 IOReadBandwidthMax='/dev/nvme0n1 100M'

check.q: How can you find which workload suffers from I/O contention?
check.a: Compare per-cgroup io.pressure values, which show stall time for each service or container.

psi-in-cgroup-v2.core: Every cgroup v2 directory has cpu.pressure, memory.pressure and io.pressure (and irq.pressure on newer kernels) with the same format as /proc/pressure, scoped to that group's tasks. That enables per-service and per-pod contention monitoring, PSI triggers on specific cgroups, systemd-oomd policies per slice (ManagedOOMMemoryPressure=kill), and Kubernetes or autoscaler decisions based on real stall time rather than utilisation.

first_principles.problem: A multi-tenant node needs to know which tenant is suffering contention, not just that the node is busy.

analogy.title: Measuring wait times per department
analogy.story: Instead of building-wide averages, each department's queue times show who's actually suffering.
analogy.breaks: Departments are fixed; cgroups appear and disappear with pods.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Batch jobs killed when their pressure exceeds 50%, protecting others.

check.a: Lets systemd-oomd kill processes in that cgroup when its memory pressure exceeds the configured limit for a sustained period.
